power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: A Systems Approach to Understanding Experiences of Primary Healthcare in Underserved Autistic Communities: Development and Evaluation of Participatory Creative Systems Mapping

text.text: Autistic people who are racially minoritised, are from areas of high economic deprivation, have co-occurring learning disabilities, or are non-or minimally-speaking are frequently excluded from autism research.
This leaves critical gaps in evidence for service development.

We addressed this by developing and evaluating "Participatory Creative Systems Mapping (PCSM)" -an emerging practice that combines Community-Based Participatory Research, Participatory Systems Mapping, and creative methods.
The novelty arises from combining these approaches to systemically reduce barriers to underserved autistic communities' participation and engagement in research.
We partnered with disability-focused and community organisations, and an autistic steering group to develop and deliver accessible workshops.

These workshops incorporated persona development, user journey mapping, storyboarding, and live artist visualisation to translate underserved autistic peoples' experiences of primary healthcare into system-level insights.
Thirty-one participants (including autistic adults and parents of autistic people) took part across four individual workshops.

The participant cohort included representation from Somali and Black African communities (35.5%), areas of high neighbourhood deprivation, and reported a variety of methods for how they usually communicate.
Autistic people with learning disabilities were represented, but this was not consistently self-reported by participants.
Evaluation indicated high satisfaction, with all respondents who provided feedback about sharing their ideas and experiences reporting that they felt able to do so in the workshops.

As proof of concept for PCSM as a method, we successfully produced a causal loop diagram reflected on by the steering group -the "Misalignment-Invalidation Cycle", illustrating how communication barriers and clinician invalidation generate reinforcing loops of misunderstanding and disengagement from healthcare.
Why was this program developed?
Autistic people are more likely to have health problems.
It can be hard for autistic people to get good healthcare.

Many autistic people are not included in research, for instance, autistic people from diverse backgrounds, particularly those from racial minority communities, deprived areas, and people with learning disabilities or communication differences.
This program was developed to help these groups take part in healthcare research.
We created a new program that combines community-based work with creative activities to explore healthcare experiences.
We designed this to be accessible for people with different communication styles, language backgrounds and support needs.
Working with Sheffield Voices (a self-advocacy group for autistic and learning-disabled people) and a steering group of six autistic adults from diverse backgrounds, we designed a workshop.
The workshop was delivered three times in partnership with different local community groups, and a fourth time with the steering group.
Participants created an autistic character and used storyboards to follow the character's journey from feeling unwell to seeing a doctor.
An artist drew these as "loops", which we used to discuss how problems (like a doctor not understanding autism) connect and feed into other issues.
We evaluated three main things.
First, to check whether we reached autistic people usually left out of research, we asked participants to tell us about their backgrounds by writing about or drawing themselves.
Second, participants told us if they felt heard during the workshops by placing feedback tokens into postboxes.

Third, to show that participants could map their healthcare experiences, we combined the artists' drawings from across the workshops into a larger, more diverse group of autistic people to see if these problems are the same across the country.
This program provides a clear guide for including diverse autistic communities in healthcare research.
By sharing findings with healthcare professionals and policymakers, we can recommend ways to improve healthcare for autistic people.
Finally, we share key methodological lessons for trust-building, flexibility, and accessibility infrastructure.

These offer a roadmap for researchers who are seeking to engage underserved autistic people in participatory, system-level inquiry. digital healthcare map and asked the steering group to reflect on whether the "loop" produced from their specific workshop actually represented their experiences.

We successfully reached participants who are usually left out of research; 31 autistic adults or their parents from diverse backgrounds took part, with many from Somali and Black African communities and areas of high deprivation.
Participants also reported a range of different ways they usually communicate.
Participants felt heard; all those who gave feedback reported being able to share their ideas and experiences in the workshop.

The program could map autistic healthcare experiences; the steering group's "loop" showed how communication differences can lead to doctors dismissing their worries, which makes an appointment feel like a waste of time, causing them anxiety and not wanting to go in the future.
The project was limited to South Yorkshire, so findings may not be the same elsewhere.
Because we relied on workshop participants to provide their own demographic information, we may not have captured how many had a learning disability.

One workshop included parents of autistic children, which mixed child and adult healthcare experiences, and we only heard about non-speaking autistic people's experiences from the people who support them.
Recruiting through community groups also meant that more socially isolated individuals may not have taken part.
Finally, the digital healthcare map needs to be taken back and checked with all community groups.
This program can help us better understand autistic experiences of healthcare and identify ways to make services more accessible.

text.text: As such, primary care offers a valuable opportunity to intervene and improve healthcare outcomes for autistic people.

Healthcare challenges are compounded for autistic people belonging to underserved groups, including those who are from racially minoritised communities, low-income backgrounds, with co-occurring learning disabilities 1 , and who are non-or minimally speaking. 23, 24 Drawing on broader minority stress theory, inequalities are both intersectional and additive for those with multiple marginalised identities. 25 For example, autistic people who are racially minoritised may also face language barriers, systemic racism, or a lack of cultural sensitivity. 26, 27 Autism research has historically centred predominantly white, cisgender, middle-class experiences. 28 Indeed, only 6% of autism research includes participants with co-occurring learning disability and 2% non-or minimally speaking individuals, 29 and 25% of autism intervention studies report participant race and ethnicity. 30 Such underrepresentation creates critical gaps in research and healthcare service development.

text.text: While considerable practice-based knowledge and adaptations likely exist, this is rarely captured, evaluated, or reported systematically, leaving those with arguably the greatest needs without robust evidence-based support.
Meaningful improvement to healthcare systems requires direct input from the communities they are intended to serve.

Although autistic involvement in research relating to healthcare is increasing, a recent systematic review found that autistic people rarely hold decision-making authority in studies claiming to be participatory. 31 To overcome these persistent barriers, autistic people must be routinely involved in system design and decisionmaking. 32 This requires not only a redistribution of power, positioning autistic people as coleaders with agency over healthcare research design, delivery, and dissemination, [33] [34] [35] but also a fundamental reconsideration of how this research is designed to accommodate diverse ways of participating.

text.text: Systems thinking offers a theoretical framework for understanding how components (such as provider behaviours, policy constraints, and patient outcomes) causally relate to one another to shape outcomes. 38

text.text: Mapping (PSM) brings together stakeholders with varied knowledge and perspectives to create a visual representation of a complex system, exploring and documenting perceived causal relations between its elements. 39 When co-led with autistic people, this participatory approach prioritises lived experience, aligning with authentic co-production. 40, 41 Crucially, this approach illuminates heterogeneity across autistic people by showing how individual differences and intersecting marginalisations interact with system-level factors to influence diverse healthcare experiences. 25 By collaboratively mapping these complexities, stakeholders can identify "leverage points" where interventions may create far-reaching positive impacts that benefit the widest range of needs.

text.text: Establishing community priorities before interventions are developed or scaled is a critical first step in science. 42, 43 While PSM is well-established in other fields such as design, 44 systems perspectives remain underutilised in autism research. 32, 45 This gap exists despite excellent examples of autistic co-production in healthcare, 46, 47 and increasing calls for system-level approaches to address health inequalities. 45, 48 However, the accessibility of PSM cannot be assumed.

text.text: Mapping complex systems is cognitively demanding, can privilege certain communication styles, and presents significant accessibility challenges for those with communication differences, co-occurring learning disability, or for whom the dominant language of research or service delivery is not their first.
Combined with pre-existing distrust of services among marginalised groups 49 , these barriers around PSM may deter autistic people from engaging at all.

text.text: As a result, the potential of PSM to capture the lived complexity of underserved autistic people's healthcare experiences has remained largely unrealised.
Existing approaches within autism research address either participation or systems-level complexity, but not both simultaneously.
This is the gap the present study directly addresses through our Participatory Creative Systems Mapping (PCSM) approach.

We argue that bringing PSM together with creative methods and a Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR) framework does not merely add accessibility as a supplementary feature, but fundamentally transforms what PSM can do and who can do it.

Creative methods, specifically storyboarding and user journey mapping, have been used successfully with autistic people, 50, 51 and in healthcare intervention development. 52 These methods offer flexible, multimodal pathways for sharing experiences and facilitating understanding, thereby challenging traditional assumptions about communication and participation in research. 53, 54 Embedded within a co-production structure that attends to capacity, biography, and access needs, they create the conditions for underserved autistic people to engage meaningfully with systems thinking.

text.text: No single component of this practice is novel in isolation.
The innovation lies in their deliberate combination, designed from the outset to reduce barriers to participation as a structural feature of the method.

The overarching aim of this emerging practices paper is to outline the development and provide a methodological evaluation of PCSM as a transferable approach for engaging underserved autistic people in system-level inquiry.
We address this by: 1.

Assessing whether underserved autistic communities (specifically autistic adults and parents of autistic people), as defined by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) INCLUDE guidance, 55 could be successfully reached and engaged; 2.

Demonstrating how the healthcare experiences of underserved autistic communities can be translated into systems-level insights.
The novelty of PCSM comes from the relationships between its constituent parts.

CBPR provides the relational and ethical foundation; creative methods offer accessible entry points for participation; and PSM translates that participation into system-level outputs, mapping the relationships between systemic factors.

Together, they address a dual methodological challenge that no single component solves: making participation genuinely accessible to underserved autistic people, while producing system-level insights capable of informing meaningful change.

text.text: The overall goal of the workshops was to translate the healthcare experiences of underserved autistic communities into systems-level insights by producing Causal Loop Diagrams (CLD) with each group.

CLDs are a core tool in systems thinking that go beyond listing problems to articulating why those problems persist by mapping the causal relationships and feedback dynamics that maintain or worsen a system's current state. 38, 39 Unlike linear representations (e.g., A → B → C), CLDs capture circular causality, in which a change in one part of the system triggers a chain of effects that ultimately feeds back to influence where it began. 64, 65 These feedback loops are classified as either reinforcing, where change compounds in the same direction (for example, inaccessible healthcare environments mean that autistic patients are less likely to attend, leading to a lower likelihood of disclosure and recording of needs, therefore fewer adaptations, and continued inaccessibility) or balancing, where forces resist or stabilise change to maintain the status quo (e.g., offering longer appointments to improve accessibility, but this increases backlog and wait times, thus leading to less available appointments, reverting the system to its original state).

text.text: To generate these CLDs, we used our PCSM approach to gather perspectives from four distinct groups, with three workshops held in community settings and one with the steering group, producing multiple views of the same system.
Each workshop had at least four facilitators (3 researchers or academics and 1 co-lead from Sheffield Voices), as well as support from the community group organisers.
We generally aimed to recruit 12 participants per workshop, in line with recommendations, 66 but group size was flexible based on interest and the size of community groups.

Creative methods were integrated throughout, as described below.

text.text: A foundational requirement in systems research with underserved communities is creating conditions where people can contribute meaningfully to abstract, analytical tasks.
Existing approaches to participatory systems mapping typically begin with an open discussion of problems and barriers.

This format is highly likely to exclude people who find unstructured verbal participation difficult, or who carry a history of trauma and marginalisation from sharing their experiences with services and not being believed, helped, or taken seriously.

Our approach addressed this via user journey mapping, which involves systematically tracing a person's experience through a service from start to finish. 68 This method is established in design and service improvement contexts but has rarely been integrated into participatory systems research, and to our knowledge, has not previously been combined with systems mapping in autism research.

text.text: Its novelty here lies not in the technique itself but in its function: user-journey mapping served as a structured, lowthreshold bridge between lived experience and systems-level analysis, translating what participants know into a form which could be directly mapped onto causal relationships between system components.
During the first hour of the workshop, participants used this approach to trace an autistic personas experience of primary healthcare.

Personas are fictional composite characters created to represent a particular group's interests and needs. 69 This approach allowed participants to discuss how they and others in their community interact with healthcare systems, encouraging them to think beyond their own experience to those who are similar.

text.text: The persona was then presented with a non-urgent healthrelated scenario describing an itchy rash that has not gone away.
We deliberately selected this as a relatable and routine health issue to keep the focus on primary care and avoid potential distress from discussing a more severe or traumatic medical event.
This was endorsed by the steering group.

User journey mapping was conducted with the persona via a storyboarding activity, providing a creative visual and narrative element to the sequence of events (see Supplemental Figure 2). 52, 69 The storyboard was presented as a matrix, with rows representing the chronological healthcare journey across five distinct steps: 1.

Booking an appointment; 3.
Travelling to the surgery; 4.
Waiting for the appointment at the surgery; and 5.
Seeing and talking to the doctor.

Columns of the storyboard template were aligned with the COM-B framework for behaviour change, 70 which posits that behaviour is generated by the interaction of Capability (psychological and physical capacity), Opportunity (external factors making behaviour possible or prompting it), and Motivation (brain processes that energise and direct behaviour).
text.formatted: Columns of the storyboard template were aligned with the COM-B framework for behaviour change, <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">70</ref> which posits that behaviour is generated by the interaction of Capability (psychological and physical capacity), Opportunity (external factors making behaviour possible or prompting it), and Motivation (brain processes that energise and direct behaviour).

text.text: This framework was chosen because navigating a healthcare system involves a complex sequence of healthcare-seeking behaviours, and COM-B ensured we captured the full range of factors driving those actions.

Crucially, COM-B was not used to suggest modifications or interventions to behaviours, but served as a taxonomy to untangle individual-level factors (Capability and Motivation) from systemic barriers (Opportunity).

For each of the five healthcare journey steps, we operationalised the COM-B components into plain language, prompting participants to identify: • Goals: What are they (i.e., the persona) trying to achieve?
• Barriers: What made it difficult for them?
• Facilitators: What helped them?
• Emotions: How did they feel?
Participants used various media to populate the storyboard, including sticky notes, stickers, and drawings, alongside verbal contributions which were scribed by the researchers.
The research team actively engaged in the workshops, exploring and clarifying the intended meaning of all storyboard additions with participants.
Two designated researchers took notes during these interactions in a shared online document, separating out the healthcare journey steps and COM-B components.
These notes digitally captured all media added and discussed, forming the raw data used to map causal relationships.
Following the storyboarding, participants voted on which step of the healthcare journey they wanted to explore in more detail by placing stickers directly onto the storyboard.

Given the limited time of the workshop, the subsequent activity would focus exclusively on this prioritised stage where participants explored the causal relationships between components for that specific part of the system.
The central methodological challenge of the workshops was bridging the gap between accessible creative participation and the technical demands of constructing a CLD.

Building a systems map from scratch is cognitively demanding, time-consuming, and typically requires prior familiarity with systems thinking. 71 To make rigorous CLD construction feasible within a single workshop session, without shifting the cognitive burden onto participants, we used a Large Language Model (LLM) and a live artist in distinct, sequential roles.

text.text: Neither replaced participant input: both served as tools for translating what participants had already contributed into a form the group could interrogate, challenge, and refine.

During the one-hour structured break, the research team collated the digital notes from the storyboarding activity, which captured participants' contributions as described above, into a structured text prompt.
The prompt instructed the LLM to reorganise these contributions into example feedback loops and plain-language summaries.

We processed this using Google Gemini, 72 specifically because the University of Sheffield's institutional data governance requirements ensured that no information entered would be stored or used to train the model.
text.formatted: We processed this using Google Gemini, <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">72</ref> specifically because the University of Sheffield's institutional data governance requirements ensured that no information entered would be stored or used to train the model.

text.text: Crucially, the LLM introduced no new content and acted purely as an administrative tool to rapidly structure what participants had already produced into a provisional framework, showing how their identified experiences might connect causally within the system.
We explicitly framed and communicated this process as a starting point for discussion, not a finished or authoritative representation of participants' experiences.
The full prompt and an example output are available in Supplemental Text 2 and 3.

The steering group and community partners reviewed and endorsed integrating the LLM into the workshop structure, but emphasised that it was critical to explain to participants how the LLM would be used and how their data would be handled.

Particular attention was given to the risk of reproducing ableist or deficit-based framings. 73 To mitigate this, the prompt imposed explicit boundaries on the LLM's output, including instructions to use only factors participants provided during the workshop and not to introduce or infer additional ones.

text.text: Following this (also in the structured break), a live artist, experienced in community workshop facilitation and present throughout the workshop, translated the LLM's example feedback loops into hand-drawn illustrations.

Research-artist collaborations are wellevidenced as a way to increase the accessibility, understandability, and communicative power of complex information. 74 Here, the artist's illustrations served a specific function: making causal relationships between system components tangible and engaging for a group that had not been asked to have any prior knowledge of systems thinking.

text.text: For example, the artist depicted CLDs as a visual narrative that participants could immediately read and respond to (see Supplemental Figure 3 for an example).

text.text: These illustrations were shared with participants immediately following the lunch break, functioning as dynamic discussion tools rather than finished outputs.
In the final part of the workshop, participants were invited to interrogate, challenge, and refine the illustrated feedback loops.
Researchers verbally walked the group through each loop, step by step, referring to the visualisations created by the live-artist.

Here, we reframe traditional qualitative concepts of "member checking" and "validation" (which position researchers as verifying the accuracy of data or analysis against participant experience) as "member reflection" to privilege ongoing, participant-led dialogue. 75 Participants assessed whether the suggested causal relationships were accurate, and identified anything that was missing, overstated, or wrongly connected.

text.text: Some participants contributed verbally, while others used gestures or added stickers to the artwork.
Engaging in this collective member reflection facilitated a shared understanding and ensured the emerging CLD was grounded in participants' lived realities, 76 rather than the LLM's.

text.text: This stage also provided a natural entry point for participants to begin identifying external drivers which might interrupt an unhelpful cycle in the loop, serving as a precursor to formally establishing leverage points.
This meant the final output was not only credible but also oriented towards potential entry points for intervention. 38

text.text: Conducting participatory research with underserved autistic people across diverse communities presents a distinct set of accessibility and inclusion challenges that standard research protocols are not designed to address.

These fall into three broad areas: 1) the cognitive and emotional demands of participation; 2) communication and interaction differences; and 3) the structural and cultural barriers that shape who feels able to engage in the first place.
The design of the workshops was shaped throughout by these challenges, informed by established recommendations for including autistic people in research.

Participatory research that asks people to reflect on difficult healthcare experiences across multiple sessions risks compounding emotional burden, particularly for those whose history with services has involved repeatedly presenting their needs and not being believed, helped, or taken seriously.
We therefore designed all activities to be completed within a single three-hour session, minimising the demands placed on participants.
Containing the work within one session also carried both methodological and emotional benefits.

Participants could reflect on how their contributions had been translated into systems-level insights while still in the room, reducing uncertainty about whether their experiences were understood and represented accurately, and ensuring oversight of the mapping remained with them.
This also enabled in-room reflections on the example feedback loops, with the creative outputs still visible and the session's discussions fresh in mind.
Real-time LLM synthesis was key to making this achievable within a single session.

When applied thoughtfully, LLMs can help mitigate time constraints while reducing cognitive burden and communication barriers for neurodivergent and other historically marginalised groups. 78, 79 While the session was structured around two hours of core activities and a one-hour break for food and refreshments, additional unstructured breaks were actively encouraged throughout.

text.text: Most participants remained engaged for the full duration, consistent with evidence that three hours represents a recommended upper limit for workshops of this kind. 66

text.text: Autistic participants may experience barriers to participation emerging from unclear verbal communication, unstructured interaction, and sensory environments.
To address this, facilitators adopted inclusive communication styles throughout, using clear, literal language, and allowing for extended processing time with regular summaries of activities.
Contribution was actively invited while the right to pass or opt out was explicitly validated.
Opportunities for one-to-one contributions were offered where space allowed, and participants were encouraged to share feedback during sessions so that needs could be accommodated in real time.

To reduce the reliance on spoken or written communication, we used a traffic light system worn on lanyards with coloured cards of green ("I am happy to join in"), yellow ("I need some support"), and red ("I need space and time"), allowing participants to signal and update their interaction preferences. 77 All research materials were provided in both standard and Easy Read formats.

text.text: At Israac, materials were also available in Somali, translated by community group members.
All workshop activities were explicitly multimodal.
For example, sticky notes, stickers, drawing, art and craft materials, and verbal contributions scribed by researchers were all ways to engage.
This ensured that being non-speaking or having language differences was not a barrier to contribution.
We also funded support workers and translators to attend where requested.
Structural and cultural factors shape not only who can attend research but who feels recognised and included within it.

We applied culturally competent recruitment and inclusion criteria, adapting our approach when it became evident that cultural differences influenced how autism was perceived and disclosed across communities. 80, 81 For instance, in the workshop delivered with the Somali community organisation, Israac, adults openly identifying as autistic were less common, but mothers felt comfortable, supported, and highly engaged when discussing the healthcare barriers that they experienced on behalf of their autistic children.

text.text: While we recognise that caregiver and autistic perspectives are fundamentally distinct, we wanted to avoid excluding these voices from communities already facing significant barriers to research participation. 26, 27 We therefore broadened our inclusion criteria for this specific workshop to welcome parents as proxy informants, valuing their experiential knowledge without conflating it directly with autistic lived experience.

text.text: Management of the physical environment was prioritised to minimise sensory demands, with workshops held in familiar community venues wherever possible.
Some spaces presented unavoidable acoustic challenges, such as high ceilings and echoing rooms, which we acknowledge as a limitation.
To enhance accessibility, a dedicated separate space was available at all workshops so that participants could take time out at any point if they wished.
Our evaluation of PCSM focused on assessing the method and process rather than outputs in isolation.

We measured success against our three core aims: 1) reaching and engaging underserved autistic communities; 2) whether they felt able to meaningfully contribute; and 3) translating their healthcare experiences into systems-level insight.
Qualitative and quantitative data were collected from both the steering group and workshop participants using methods designed to minimise participant burden.
These data sources were explicitly mapped to our three aims:

Beyond our targeted recruitment of organisations serving underserved communities, we assessed our overall reach by measuring the self-reported demographic diversity of workshop participants against the NIHR INCLUDE framework. 55 Success was therefore defined as the active engagement of underserved autistic communities in the PCSM workshops, specifically those that are racially minoritised, living in areas of high economic deprivation, have a learning disability and/or who are non-or minimally speaking.

text.text: This included both direct participation from autistic adults, and parents sharing the experiences of their autistic child in one workshop where this was the preference of a community.
To collect the demographic data of those who participated, we used an accessible "Blank
Character" template rather than a standard questionnaire.

This was presented at the end of the workshop and featured a character outline surrounded by questions with open-ended text boxes (see Supplemental Figure 4), allowing participants to report aspects of their identity they felt important to share (e.g., ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and co-occurring conditions) in their own words or by drawing.

text.text: The accessibility and inclusivity of the PSCM workshop process were captured by evaluating whether participants understood the session's purpose, felt valued, and felt able to contribute.
We adopted an interactive, low-burden form of evaluation using a physical "Postbox" system at the end of the workshop (see Supplemental Figure 5).
text.formatted: We adopted an interactive, low-burden form of evaluation using a physical "Postbox" system at the end of the workshop (see Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>).

text.text: Participants gave feedback by placing tokens with faces (Happy, Neutral, Sad) into 5 postboxes to indicate their rating on a 3-point Likert Scale, with the option to leave open-ended comments.

Each postbox displayed a different evaluation question designed to map onto a domain from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR; see Supplemental Table 5). 83, 84 CFIR provides a well-established, theory-informed structure for examining the multilevel factors that shape whether an innovation (i.e., PCSM) can be effectively implemented.

text.text: It highlights key barriers and facilitators across five interconnected domains:

Innovation Characteristics (features of the innovation itself, such as complexity and adaptability), Outer Setting (external context and influences on implementation), Inner Setting (organisational context, including culture, communication, and resources), Individuals (characteristics of those involved, including knowledge, beliefs, and motivation), and Implementation Process (strategies and activities used to plan, execute, and refine implementation).
We calculated descriptive statistics of Likert responses, and qualitative comments were compiled and summarised, with exemplar quotes reported.
We sought to provide proof of concept for PCSM as a method by demonstrating that participants' lived healthcare experiences could be feasibly translated into systems-level insights.

To do this, the researchers synthesised the live artist's hand-drawn feedback loops into a cross-workshop systems map, focusing exclusively on the feedback loops participants voted to prioritise and reflect on in each workshop.
These loops were digitised into CLDs using Kumu, 85 a relationship-mapping software, by drafting the initial components and causal relationships from the artwork.

We cross-referenced this against researcher notes, audio recordings, and storyboards, using CFIR domains to guide our interpretation of the systemic barriers and facilitators to healthcare access raised by participants.
The research team then collaboratively refined and adjusted component names and the direction of connections to ensure they faithfully reflected what was shared by the group.

External drivers (i.e. factors that influence a component of the map but are not influenced by it) discussed by participants were also incorporated as incoming components, 39 indicating community priorities for change (i.e., potential leverage points for intervention).

text.text: Established PSM approaches would then typically involve another round of member reflection. 66, 86 However, within the project constraints, we could only present the steering group's digitised CLD back to them for this extended process.

text.text: We systematically reviewed each component and causal relationship together, and steering group members confirmed or refined these elements using their preferred communication methods, such as talking, writing on printouts, or typing.

While the resulting cross-workshop, researcher-synthesised map is provided as a supplementary resource for interactive viewing in Kumu (see Supplemental Link 1), it is not necessary to understand the core messages of the paper.
Instead, we focus on the specific CLD generated by the autistic steering group as our primary "proof of concept.

The cohort included substantial representation from racially minoritised groups, with 35.5% (n = 11) self-or proxy-reporting as Somali or Black African, and from areas of neighbourhood economic deprivation with a median IMD decile of 2 (Range: 1 [lowest] -9 [highest]).
The most frequently reported IMD deciles in the total sample were 1 (n= 9, 29%) and 2 (n = 8, 25.8%).

Participants reported a variety of communication methods beyond primarily speaking (e.g., body language, written text, sign language; n = 15, 48.4%), but only four parents proxy-reported their autistic child as non-or minimally speaking (12.9%).

Likewise, although we partnered with a learning disability service (Burton Street Foundation) for one workshop and autistic adults with co-occurring learning disabilities participated, only one person self-reported this (3.2%).

text.text: Overall, participant engagement and satisfaction were high.
Twenty-two participants (95.7%) confirmed they understood the workshop's purpose, with one participant (4.3%) indicating they understood "a bit".
The majority, 19 participants (86.4%), rated the workshop as "good", with 3 (13.6%) rating it as "okay".

Crucially, for the assessment of accessibility of the co-production process, all participants who answered the question (100%; n = 20) felt able to share their ideas and experiences during their session.

text.text: For the open-ended qualitative feedback regarding the workshops, participants specifically highlighted the inclusive environment, noting the value of "fidgets and multiple forms of communication", "people translating my views", and being afforded "plenty of time for processing and speaking".
The presence of a live artist was a recurring highlight; as one participant noted, "I loved all the posters that were being drawn... [the participant] wanted to take them all home".
Feeling validated was central to the workshop's success.
Participants expressed that they "felt heard" and appreciated "being given time to discuss issues".
This allowed for a shared exploration of "issues and barriers our community experiences" through "group work, and meeting with other Autistic people who have similar experiences and understanding".
Suggestions for improvement primarily addressed structure and facilitation.

Participants recommended practical adjustments such as "text reminders on the day", ensuring "toilets are nearby", and making sessions more accessible by ensuring all questions are "not just written down, but also read".

One participant desired "a little more structure and keeping people on topic", noting that while the session "felt logically set out to begin with, [it] quickly went all over the place" and felt they "might have had more to say on each section" if this had been maintained.

When reflecting on the most important thing they learnt for themselves, participants' key takeaways included "learning about other people's experiences and highlighting the common experiences that we shared", "having others that understand", realising they are "not alone", and that "my experiences matter".

The workshop also provided practical empowerment for some, where one participant "found a communication aid that I feel will be useful", while another resolved to "try not to be as anxious when I visit the doctor's surgery".
To provide proof of concept for the PCSM method, we present the CLD that was generated, reflected on and refined by the steering group (see Figure 3).

The resulting CLD captures structural complexity and feedback dynamics that would not otherwise be visible, demonstrating the merit of our innovative methodology.
Furthermore, PCSM enabled participants to identify potential priorities for disrupting unhelpful feedback loops.

text.text: The value of PCSM is most clearly shown in the primary reinforcing loop.

The cycle starts with Communication Barriers experienced by the autistic person (i.e., service user), such as communication differences or difficulties identifying and describing how they feel Furthermore, PCSM showed a reciprocal relationship between Appointment Preparation Support and the Ability to Self-Advocate.
Tools that help the autistic person prepare for the appointment (e.g., symptom diaries or having questions in advance) enable them to advocate for themselves.
At the same time, when the autistic person is able to self-advocate, they feel more confident using these preparation tools.
However, this relationship relies heavily on Available Energy (or "Spoons") 87 as a key driver.
text.formatted: However, this relationship relies heavily on Available Energy (or "Spoons") <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">87</ref> as a key driver.

text.text: If the autistic person's Ability to Self-Advocate is constantly undermined, they reach a state of Disempowerment, which can cause them to stop using the healthcare system entirely.
A methodological strength of PCSM is that it can identify priorities for change, rather than just simply pointing out problems.

As shown, Clear and Accessible Communication (e.g., providing written information, avoiding jargon, and easy-read formats) helps reduce both Recall Challenges and Misaligned Understanding of Symptoms by supporting the autistic person to remember relevant information and answer questions.

Similarly, providing Alternative Communication Methods (e.g., typing on a phone, using text-to-speech) improves Misaligned Understanding of Symptoms as the autistic person can choose to communicate in the way that works best for them.
Finally, the clinician's attitude plays a vital role.
Clinician Bias/Prejudice (i.e., making assumptions based on a person being autistic or their appearance) contributes to Clinician Dismissal/Invalidation.
In contrast, Clinician Warmth and Receptivity can break the negative cycle, reducing dismissal and creating more equitable care.
When engaging with traditionally underserved and marginalised communities, researchers must move beyond rigid project timelines to embrace a flexible, relational approach to co-production.
Drawing on our experience from this project, we offer two key recommendations to guide meaningful engagement with underserved autistic populations in participatory research.

Meaningful engagement with underserved groups relies heavily on cultivating relational networks and an appropriate approach, in addition to sufficient time and resources (cited as the main barriers to engaging underserved groups by professionals in the UK). 88 This type of community work fundamentally "moves at the speed of relationships".
text.formatted: Meaningful engagement with underserved groups relies heavily on cultivating relational networks and an appropriate approach, in addition to sufficient time and resources (cited as the main barriers to engaging underserved groups by professionals in the UK). <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">88</ref> This type of community work fundamentally "moves at the speed of relationships".

text.text: Our project was co-led with a community partner (Sheffield Voices), building upon a relationship established well before the grant-writing phase.
During the year of the project, we visited and engaged with community groups multiple times before data collection began, holding information sessions and attending community events.

This duration was necessary to move beyond transactional research and towards genuine, long-term relationships. 33 Throughout this process, the research team also engaged in reflexive practice through regular team discussions to examine our own positionality and address any implicit biases held from an outsider perspective. 89 Resource allocation is also essential to cover the costs associated with accessibility.

text.text: We funded support workers and translators to attend workshops, both of which were required so participants could meaningfully share their experiences in their preferred language or with necessary accommodations.
Community groups operate in a dynamic environment that can conflict with the rigid processes of academic research.
Success required us to relinquish control and let the community groups guide the pace and format of engagement where feasible.

Practically, this meant conducting sessions in familiar community spaces rather than university settings and organising workshops around school or childcare commitments. 33, 88 Promoting agency meant respecting community boundaries and organisational capacity.
text.formatted: Practically, this meant conducting sessions in familiar community spaces rather than university settings and organising workshops around school or childcare commitments. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">88</ref> Promoting agency meant respecting community boundaries and organisational capacity.

text.text: For example, our intention had been to work with autistic adults directly within each community group, but at Israac, the Somalian community centre, we instead worked with parents as proxy informants for their children, as this was the preference of the group.
We also recognised that not every attempt at engagement would succeed.

Despite our best efforts and the support of our community partner, one group stepped back after initial meetings, and we were unable to find a time that worked for another group despite willingness on both sides.

Community groups may be overstretched, under-resourced, have competing priorities, or simply may not perceive the immediate value of the proposed research. 89 Researchers must therefore remain mindful of not only avoiding extractive relationships, but also depletive ones, recognising that research involvement can draw heavily from an organisation's finite capacities.

text.text: Respecting these boundaries and reassuring partners that they can step back without consequence is an essential part of maintaining a respectful and ethical relationship.
In this paper, we describe and evaluate PCSM, an innovative emerging practice that combines CBPR with PSM and creative methods.
Our evaluation demonstrated that meaningful engagement with underserved autistic people is achievable but requires more than just adequate resourcing (i.e., time and accessibility budgets).
Success resulted from working in partnership with community organisations and taking a relational approach grounded in continued listening and trust-building.

By utilising multimodal contribution via the creative methods of persona development, storyboarding, and live artist visualisation, PCSM was accessible to diverse communication styles and first languages.
This approach allowed for real-time, intuitive member reflection on components and causal relationships.

Crucially, we demonstrated that all respondents who gave feedback on sharing their ideas and experiences felt able to do so, implying that the integration of creative methods successfully mitigated the cognitive and verbal demands that standard systems mapping can typically impose.

Beyond the methodological success of PCSM as a viable approach for participatory research with underserved autistic people, the steering group's "Clinical Misalignment Invalidation Cycle" CLD provides a participant-informed reflection of how structural features of healthcare systems can produce reinforcing patterns of misunderstanding, avoidance, and disengagement.
By making these structural failures visible, PCSM challenges deficit-based views of autistic people, which typically place the blame on the individual without considering the wider context.

Instead, barriers such as Misaligned Understanding of Symptoms may arise from inadequate autism-specific provider training and insufficient support for autistic people to communicate in ways that work for them. 20 The Double Empathy Problem offers a useful framework for understanding this misalignment, highlighting how differences in communication and interpretation between autistic and non-autistic people contribute to a mutual breakdown in understanding. 90, 91 In healthcare settings, these difficulties can compound into a Triple Empathy Problem, as medical jargon, assumptions and institutional structures create additional barriers to shared perspective-taking between autistic patients and non-autistic doctors, further marginalising autistic people. 92 Within this system-level insight, the external drivers identified in the "Clinical Misalignment Invalidation Cycle" causal loop function as the steering group's priorities for disrupting the reinforcing loop.

text.text: Consequently, this offers both policymakers and healthcare professionals targeted areas to explore for potential service improvements.

While many of the identified barriers manifest as behaviours and practices, shifting them at scale will require broader policy implications, such as the need to structurally mandate, fund and support coordinated and multidisciplinary action to achieve systemic change.

A key strength of this project lies in the authentic co-production we achieved with our community partner and the steering group, which was maintained throughout the lifecycle of the project. 40, 56 This partnership addresses field-wide issues with the depth of autistic involvement in participatory research, as our multi-level engagement spanned from identifying the initial research question through to study design, data analysis, and paper writing. 31 Furthermore, formal evaluation of the co-production process is rare in autism research.

text.text: By embedding evaluation into the development of PCSM, we gathered perspectives on inclusion and accessibility within the workshops, providing a transparent assessment of our approach.

We achieved a level of engagement and sample size appropriate for PSM workshops, 66 while capturing intersections of race and neighbourhood deprivation that are systematically underrepresented in autism research. 30 This highlights that when methodology is culturally and structurally adapted to community needs, underserved groups are willing and able to contribute complex systemic insights.

text.text: Moreover, by following the GRIPP2 and GUIDED checklists, 57, 67 we also ensured transparency and consistency in reporting both our emerging practice and co-production processes.

text.text: Despite these strengths, several limitations must be acknowledged.
The project was geographically localised to South Yorkshire (specifically Sheffield and Rotherham).

This was an intentional methodological choice to facilitate meaningful and trusted engagement by leveraging existing community and voluntary sector infrastructure in these ethnically and socially diverse localities. [58] [59] [60] While we successfully developed and evaluated the PCSM methodology with a range of underserved autistic communities, healthcare access in the UK varies significantly due to regional commissioning differences (commonly known as the "postcode lottery"). 95 Consequently, our current mapping outputs may confound universal systemic experiences with localised service dynamics.

text.text: Future applications of PCSM would therefore benefit from a wider geographical reach to distinguish universal systemic barriers from local service configurations.
Additionally, recruitment relied heavily on autistic people already engaged with community organisations, likely excluding individuals who are more socially isolated.

This represents an important challenge, given the established association between social isolation, loneliness, and poorer health outcomes. 96 Limitations were also evident in the representation of participants with co-occurring learning disability and non-or minimally speaking populations.
text.formatted: This represents an important challenge, given the established association between social isolation, loneliness, and poorer health outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">96</ref> Limitations were also evident in the representation of participants with co-occurring learning disability and non-or minimally speaking populations.

text.text: Although the sample included a diverse range of communication styles and our use of creative methods allowed for multimodal contributions, we only heard about the experiences of non-and minimally speaking autistic people from parents acting as proxy informants (12.9%).

While valuable, proxy accounts are distinct from the lived experience of autistic people and should not be relied on exclusively. 24 Through reflexive discussions with the wider research team and steering group, we recognise that not proactively and visibly integrating a broader range of Augmentative and Alternative Communication tools (e.g., Makaton, symbol boards) into the workshop design may have been an unintended barrier to inclusion.

text.text: Non-speaking autistic people and those who support them may have assumed the workshops were "not for them", contributing to their absence.
Moreover, parent proxies within the Somali community group introduced paediatric healthcare perspectives alongside adult experiences, blending two structurally distinct healthcare systems.
Demographic data also indicated low self-report of learning disability despite recruitment from community groups specifically serving this population.
This likely reflects a trade-off between our co-produced materials and standardised data collection.

The "Blank Character" form was designed to be accessible and sensitive to underserved identities by encouraging participants to self-identify "other developmental conditions" rather than explicitly asking about learning disabilities. 97 This may have led to under-reporting of relevant demographics.

text.text: Future work should consider further refinements to demographic measures to better capture learning disability and communication differences without compromising on the inclusive ethos of the work.
Finally, we must distinguish between the feasibility of generating CLDs and conducting extended member reflection across a full systems map.

While our steering group engaged in member reflection to refine the "Clinical Misalignment" CLD as a proof of concept, within the scope of the current project we were unable to extend this process to the other community groups' CLDs or the consolidated cross-workshop map.
Consequently, the latter currently represents a researcher-led synthesis based on our interpretations of the data.

Participatory systems mapping relies on relational and qualitative processes to assess how faithfully a map represents the system of interest. 98 This requires re-engaging community groups for evidence triangulation or "disconfirmation", as well as testing causal relationships and leverage points with wider stakeholders.

text.text: Future iterations of PCSM must factor in the substantial additional time and resources required for this extended member reflection before a map is used to inform or develop policy, service design or systems-level interventions. 66

text.text: The value of PCSM extends beyond just healthcare.

Medical systems interface dynamically with housing, employment, education, and justice. 99 As autistic people disproportionately rely on these interconnected systems, 10 inaccessibility in one sector can ripple into others, creating a compounding ecosystem of exclusion. 100, 101 PCSM should be applied across sectors, moving beyond isolated service silos to capture the full, complex reality of autistic people's experiences. 45 Moreover, as methodologies such as PCSM are applied more widely and research practices become more inclusive, the definition of who is underserved will inevitably shift.

text.text: Researchers must therefore remain reflexive and responsive to the perspectives which remain absent.

To move from proof of concept to actionable recommendations, future work should also proactively couple PCSM with implementation science frameworks during the formative development of system-level interventions.

Specifically, CFIR can be used to anticipate multi-level factors across both outer (e.g., funding structures) and inner settings (e.g., organisational culture) from the outset, ensuring that resulting interventions are viable, sustainable, and effectively implemented. 83, 84

text.text: In this paper, we established PCSM as an innovative methodology that combines CBPR and PSM with creative methods.
Through community partnerships, we provided an actionable roadmap for participatory research with underserved autistic people that can generate high-quality, systems-level insights.
Ultimately, PCSM offers a pathway to close the research-implementation gap, driving the shift toward a healthcare system that is not only accessible but fundamentally equitable.

This can lead to a Misaligned Understanding of Symptoms, where a clinician views the autistic person as being vague, when in reality, they may not remember specific details of their health concern or what they wanted to say in the appointment (Recall Challenges).
Because of this, Clinician Dismissal/Invalidation occurs, where the autistic person's symptoms are downplayed or ignored.

The autistic person then experiences the appointment as a Perceived Waste of Time (Futility), which creates a Negative Emotional Impact on them where they may feel shame, self-blame, or anger and frustration at the healthcare system.
As a result, the autistic person has a Reluctance to Seek Care/Avoidance in the future when they are unwell.
If they do seek care, they experience Anticipatory Anxiety, often worrying about and imagining all the potential negative outcomes.
This anxiety worsens the original Communication Barriers in their next encounter, closing and strengthening the negative loop.
Beyond the main cycle, PCSM helped reveal the hidden mental effort required from the autistic person during this process.

When a Misaligned Understanding of Symptoms occurs, it increases the autistic person's Information Processing/Cognitive Load because they must work much harder to translate their experience into medical terms while also trying to understand complex questions from a clinician.
This creates a cognitive drain that reduces the autistic person's Ability to Self-Advocate, as they don't have the mental energy needed to speak up or challenge Clinician Dismissal/Invalidation.
